42: How should C, F, D, V and X barb expansion ranges be used?
43: FOREACH C, F, D, V and X barb profiles and expansion ranges
44: C/F/D/V/X identify profiles. Ranges describe their dimensional characteristics; the series references are not pressure classes.
45: Ranges overlap: F is 25%–32%, D is 24%–50%. Do not assign 50% to every D fitting or 25% to every F fitting. Calculate each termination from its drawing crest OD and the actual tubing ID.
46: Equal percentages do not guarantee equal fit. Lead-in, crest shape, tube-contact section behind the crest and surface condition affect insertion and contact. The tubing must conform effectively behind the crest; maximum OD alone misses this sealing and retention relationship.

67: Nominal dimensions conceal batch-to-batch fit variation. A smaller tubing ID increases calculated expansion; a larger ID reduces it. Include both dimension limits if crest OD also has a tolerance.

79: Does higher barb expansion always improve sealing and retention?
80: No percentage is universally 'better'. A larger crest requires greater deformation for the same tubing. Difficult insertion, cuts or permanent flaring can make a tighter nominal fit unreliable. Lower expansion is not automatically a failure either; assess contact behind the crest and performance in service.

98: How do you validate a barb-to-tubing fit?
99: Fix the complete fitting model and tubing specification, then compare candidates under actual conditions. Assemble the two BL profiles with tubing from the same batch. Avoid changing material, wall thickness and assembly method simultaneously, which obscures the cause of differences.
100: Assembly: record ease and completeness of insertion, cuts and abnormal deformation. For force measurements, fix speed, fixture and method.
101: Sealing: test with the target fluid, temperature and pressure; also check air ingress under vacuum on suction lines.
102: Retention: assess loosening under actual tensile loads, vibration and start/stop conditions. Specify clamp position and size when used.
103: After service: repeat leakage, displacement, retention and point-of-use flow checks after the agreed operating duration or cleaning cycles.

110: Can Shore hardness determine the required expansion?
111: No. Hardness helps order trials—for example, start lower with harder TPU—but cannot be converted directly into a fixed percentage. Fix tubing grade, ID/OD, tolerances and assembly conditions; confirm undamaged insertion and validate sealing and retention with the actual fluid, temperature and pressure.
112: Do I still need to check expansion when using a hose clamp?
113: Yes. A clamp changes external restraint, not the need for correct ID, profile and material matching. Select it for the assembled OD and available clamping position; include it in sealing, retention and tube-wall damage checks.
114: Can the original calculation be reused after removing the tubing?
115: The original calculation uses unassembled ID. A removed tube end may be flared, damaged or permanently deformed. Inspect or replace it according to maintenance requirements and revalidate. Consider a dedicated separable connection for frequent disconnection.
